opus-5.5.text:
I think the main value of GATE is that it forces you to be explicit about your assumptions. A lot of discussion about AI and its economic impact happens at the level of vibes. People say AI will transform everything, or that it will be overhyped, and it's hard to tell what's actually driving the disagreement. With a model like GATE, you have to pin down specific parameters. How much compute do you think is needed to automate all the tasks in the economy? How quickly does hardware get cheaper? How much do algorithmic improvements substitute for compute? How elastic is investment in response to AI's returns? Once you've written those numbers down, you can see what follows from them, and you can see which assumptions the conclusions are most sensitive to.

So the way I'd like people to use it is as a tool for locating cruxes. If you and someone else disagree about whether we'll see explosive growth this century, you can both go into the model, plug in your own parameters, and find out whether you actually disagree about the compute requirements for automation, or about how fast investment can scale, or about bottlenecks from tasks that are hard to automate. That's much more productive than arguing about the conclusion directly.

I'd also caution against treating the model's default outputs as a forecast. It's a simplified picture of the world. It leaves out a lot of things that matter, like regulatory responses, the details of how physical capital gets built, and frictions in deploying AI across firms. The headline numbers it produces can look very dramatic, and I don't think people should take those at face value. What I'd rather people take away is the qualitative dynamics. For example, if AI can substitute for labor broadly, the feedback loop between output, reinvestment in compute, and further automation can be very powerful. And the economy may be bottlenecked by whichever tasks are automated last.

Ideally it gets people asking "what would I have to believe for this outcome to happen?" rather than just "will this outcome happen?" If it shifts the conversation in that direction, it's done its job.

r001.rationale: The response says GATE’s default outputs should not be treated as a forecast and describes it as a simplified model.

r002.rationale: It describes entering parameters into GATE to see what follows and discusses the resulting dynamics, while noting that the model leaves out real-world factors.

r003.rationale: It says GATE can help people locate cruxes and identify whether they disagree about assumptions such as compute requirements or investment scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that GATE is not meant to be a forecast in the sense of "here is what's going to happen." It's a model, and the point of a model is to make your assumptions explicit and to see what follows from them when you put them together consistently. A lot of the discourse around AI and the economy, I think, suffers from people having a bunch of intuitions in their head that are actually inconsistent with each other, and they don't notice because they never write them down and check.

So one way I'd like people to use it is just as a consistency check. If you believe, say, that AI is going to be able to automate most cognitive tasks within ten or fifteen years, and you also believe that economic growth is going to stay at two or three percent per year over that period, those two things are very hard to reconcile. And when you actually try to build a model where both of those are true, you find you have to make some pretty strange assumptions about, for example, what happens to capital accumulation, or how substitutable compute is for human labor, or how fast investment responds to returns. GATE forces you to confront that. You can go in, change the parameters to reflect your own views, and see what the model says. And often what people find is that the outcomes they expected require parameter values they don't actually believe.

The second thing is that it helps you see which assumptions matter. There are a lot of inputs to the model, but the output is very sensitive to a handful of them and pretty insensitive to most of the rest. For instance, how much compute it takes to get to full automation, and how fast you can scale up compute production, those matter enormously. Some details about the exact shape of the automation curve matter much less than you might think. So if you're trying to figure out what to pay attention to, what research to do, what evidence would actually change your mind, the model can tell you where the leverage is. That's useful even if you don't trust the central estimates at all.

And then the third thing, which I think is maybe underrated, is that it gives you a sense of the dynamics rather than just endpoints. People tend to talk about AI in terms of "when do we get AGI," as if it's a single moment. But if you run the model, you see that there's a long period where AI is a significant contributor to the economy before it's doing everything, and during that period investment is ramping up, compute is scaling, growth is accelerating gradually and then more quickly. The transition is a process, and the process has structure. Understanding that structure matters for policy, for investment decisions, for thinking about what the world looks like in 2030 versus 2035.

What I'd caution against is treating the outputs as predictions with any kind of precision. The uncertainty is enormous, and the model has lots of simplifications. It doesn't model geopolitics, it doesn't really model regulation, it treats the world as a single economy. So the right attitude is something like: this is a tool for disciplining your thinking, not for replacing it. If the model tells you something surprising, the right response is to figure out why, and then decide whether you believe the mechanism or whether you think the model is missing something. Either way you've learned something, and that's really what it's for.

r001.rationale: The response says GATE is “not meant to be a forecast” and cautions against treating its outputs as predictions.

r002.rationale: It describes using GATE to make assumptions explicit and see what follows when they are combined consistently, including by examining the model’s mechanisms and dynamics.

r003.rationale: It says GATE can act as a consistency check and gives beliefs about rapid automation and slow economic growth as hard to reconcile.

astra-6.text:
I think GATE is most useful as a way of making your assumptions explicit. When people disagree about the future of AI, it can be difficult to tell whether they disagree about how quickly capabilities will improve, how expensive deployment will be, or how readily those capabilities will translate into economic output. A model gives you a way to separate those questions and see how they interact.

So I would encourage people to vary the assumptions, rather than just look at a headline result. Can you get a substantially different outcome with assumptions you still find plausible? Which assumptions do you have to change? That tells you something about where your uncertainty really lies, and what evidence would be useful for resolving it.

But you also have to ask what the model leaves out. There’s a difference between understanding why a model produces a result and having good reasons to expect that result in the world. Ideally, GATE should help people have more precise disagreements and understand the implications of their own views, while remaining open to the possibility that the model’s framing is missing something important.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a model’s results from reasons to expect them in the world, but does not state that GATE is not intended to be predictive.

r002.rationale: It says a model can separate assumptions and show how questions interact, but does not describe exploring outcomes within a simulated world from the mechanisms included in GATE.

r003.rationale: It encourages making assumptions explicit and varying them, but does not explain that GATE can expose incompatibilities among a person’s beliefs about AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful way to use GATE is as a way of making your assumptions explicit and exploring their consequences, rather than as something that gives you the answer about what’s going to happen with AI.

You might have an intuition that progress is going to be very fast, or that some bottleneck is going to slow things down. Putting that intuition into a model forces you to be more precise: What exactly is the bottleneck? How strong does it have to be? And if you change that assumption, does your conclusion survive?

I’d encourage people to look at a range of scenarios and ask which assumptions are doing the work. If someone disagrees with a result, the productive next step is to identify what they would change and see how much difference it makes. Ideally, that helps turn a broad disagreement about AI into a more concrete disagreement that we can reason about, and perhaps resolve with better evidence.

r001.rationale: It says GATE should make assumptions explicit and explore consequences rather than give an answer about what will happen with AI.

r002.rationale: It discusses exploring consequences in a model, but does not describe a simulated world or the consequences of the mechanisms included in that model.

r003.rationale: It says to identify assumptions and test whether conclusions survive, but does not clearly state that GATE can expose incompatibilities among a person's AI beliefs.
